target_customer: Nigerian millennials and small businesses needing digital wallets, transfers and bill payments; later cross border and crypto enabled users via the Spring wallet.
problem: Banked and unbanked Nigerians had slow, costly ways to pay, transfer money, pay bills and withdraw cash, and businesses lacked simple digital banking tools.
business_model: Payments and wallet fees (transfers, bill payments, cards, business banking), later multi currency wallet

founders.name: John Oke
founders.background_notes: Lagos based software engineer; conceived the wallet idea while at SureGifts per Techpoint 2020. The company says it has been backed by YC since Winter 2019.

competitors.name: Paga
competitors.what: Nigerian mobile wallet and agent network, founded 2009

competitors.name: Flutterwave
competitors.what: Payments infrastructure for businesses in Africa

competitors.name: Paystack
competitors.funding_then: 8 million Series A reported in 2019 coverage

technical_complexity.rationale: Wallet, transfers and bill payment aggregation on bank partner APIs is standard fintech engineering with compliance and reliability as the hard parts.

defensibility.rationale: Wallets and transfers were crowded and low switching cost; the licence and bank rails were rented rather than owned.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Large fintechs pushed into consumer products over 2019 to 2023; no source shows a takeover of this company.

market_need_then: Nigerian digital payments were growing fast in 2018 and 2019 and TechCrunch reported six of seven Africa focused YC Winter 2019 companies were fintech, showing investor and user interest.

branding.domain_note: Started as wallet.ng (a .ng domain); later brands use springinafrica.com. No purchase story found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Aspirational: 'Leap into tomorrow's banking', stressing secure, transparent, robust.

rebrands.why: Reported around the YC batch, reason not stated.
Product launch described as aligned with making finance accessible to all.
Reported by a secondary profile site; no primary announcement found.

brand_strength.rationale: Three name changes in five years and no brand press beyond product coverage; the Spring in Africa name now reads like an investment firm, and the company's own site tagline 'Investing in innovation' mixes two positions.

pivots.from: Naira focused Nigerian wallet and transfers
pivots.to: Multi currency Spring wallet with stablecoin and Ether features
pivots.why: Stated aim was to make finance accessible; broader product repositioning toward crypto and cross border.

outcome_analysis: Wallet.ng launched in 2016 and entered YC in Winter 2019 as Wallets Africa, then raised an undisclosed 2020 seed from Mozilla, 9Yards, Samurai Incubate and Michael Seibel. It faced much larger Nigerian fintechs, renamed itself again in 2023 and 2024, and one later commentary lists it among struggling ventures, though that claim is unverified and the YC page still shows it Active. Traction is hard to confirm because user figures come from promotional profiles, so the outcome is stalled or unclear rather than failed.
notes: Funding amount undisclosed in 2020 coverage. A 2023 TechCabal piece cites a 1.6 million dollar total and CB Insights lists 150 thousand over four rounds with a May 2019 seed; both are unverified and conflict, so they are not recorded as rounds. Traction claims (250,000 wallets, 7 million monthly volume) come from promotional yespress.io pages and are unverified. The TechCrunch demo day article URL returned 404 on fetch, so its content is cited from search snippets only. Competitor funding figures come from search snippets of 2019 and 2020 articles, not fetched pages. The commentary claiming collapse from mismanagement was seen only in a snippet and is not relied on. Company website springinafrica.com shows placeholder statistics. Spring in Africa presents itself partly as an investor, which does not match the wallet business; the entity relationship is unclear.
